name: Linux — Credential File Modified (/etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, /etc/group)
description:
Attacker objective
Establish persistence or escalate privileges on a Linux host by adding a backdoor account, changing a password hash, or granting sudo rights — i.e., modifying the core credential and authorization files.

Attack logic
On Linux, /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, /etc/group and /etc/sudoers define accounts, password hashes and privilege. An unexpected modification to these files can plant a backdoor user, reset a password, or grant elevated rights.

Why this detection works
File-integrity monitoring records write/rename events to these exact credential files, so any change to them is a high-signal, security-relevant event even without process context.

False positives
Legitimate user administration, password changes, or configuration-management/patch tooling that edits these files.

Tuning
Allowlist verified user-management and configuration-management workflows/hosts; prioritise servers where account changes are rare; correlate with the host's authentication and shell activity (which FIM does not capture).

Required telemetry
File Integrity Monitoring (fim.event): file.path, event.action, file.hash, host.name. Note: FIM does not record the process or user that made the change.
author: raadabujaish
note:
## Investigation guide
1. file.path identifies the credential file and host.name the system; FIM does not show who or which process changed it.
2. Pivot to the host's auth/shell logs (system.auth/auditd) to identify the actor and whether a backdoor account or sudo grant was added.
3. If unexplained, treat as persistence/privilege escalation and investigate the host.
false_positives: Legitimate user administration, password changes, or configuration-management/patch tooling that edits these files.
query: event.dataset:"fim.event" and event.action:("created" or "updated" or "moved") and file.path:("/etc/passwd" or "/etc/shadow" or "/etc/group" or "/etc/sudoers")
